ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *gāną Proto-West Germanic *gān Old English gān Middle English gon English go From Middle English gon, goon, from Old English gān (“to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”). The inherited past tense form yode (compare Old English ēode) was replaced through suppletion in the 15th century by went, from Old English wendan (“to go, depart, wend”).
Japanese 碁bor. English go From Japanese 碁(ご) (go), shorter variant of Japanese 囲碁(いご) (igo), from Chinese 圍棋 /围棋 (wéiqí, literally “encirclement board game”).

senses.d: To move through space (especially to or through a place). (May be used of tangible things such as people or cars, or intangible things such as moods or information.)
ex: Why don’t you go with us?
This train goes through Cincinnati on its way to Chicago.

senses.d: To move or travel through time (either literally—in a fictional or hypothetical situation in which time travel is possible—or in one's mind or knowledge of the historical record). (See also go back.)
ex: Yesterday was the second-wettest day on record; you have to go all the way back to 1896 to find a day when more rain fell.
Fans want to see the Twelfth Doctor go to the 51st century to visit River in the library.

senses.d: To navigate (to a file or folder on a computer, a site on the internet, a memory, etc.).
ex: For the best definitions, go to wiktionary.org
To access Office-related TechNet resources, go to www.microsoft.com/technet/prodtechnol/office.

senses.d: To move (a particular distance, or in a particular fashion).
ex: We've only gone twenty miles today.
This car can go circles around that one.

senses.d: To move or travel in order to do something, or to do something while moving.
ex: We went swimming.
Let's go shopping.

senses.d: To leave; to move away.
ex: Please don't go!
I really must be going.

senses.d: To follow or proceed according to (a course or path).
ex: Let's go this way for a while.
She was going that way anyway, so she offered to show him where it was.

senses.d: To travel or pass along.
ex: We went the full length of the promenade before we found a place to sit down.
His life story goes the gamut, from poverty-stricken upbringing to colossal wealth.

senses.d: To walk; to travel on one's feet.
ex: ‘As for that,’ seyde Sir Trystram, ‘I may chose othir to ryde othir to go.’
Master Piercie our new President, was so sicke hee could neither goe nor stand.

senses.d: To work or function (properly); to move or perform (as required).
ex: The engine just won't go anymore.
Don't put your hand inside while the motor's going!

senses.d: The act of going.
ex: They talk easily together and they hear the come and go of the breeze in the soon to be turning burnt leaves of the high trees.

senses.d: A turn at something, or in something (e.g. a game).
ex: You’ve been on that pinball machine long enough—now let your brother have a go.
It’s your go.

senses.d: An attempt, a try.
ex: I’ll give it a go.
You have to stay and we will have a go at winning the championship next season."

senses.d: A period of activity.
ex: ate it all in one go

senses.d: A time; an experience.
A circumstance or occurrence; an incident, often unexpected.
ex: “Ain't this a rum go? This is a queer sort of dodge for lighting the streets.”
“It’s a rum go and no mistake.”

senses.d: An approval or permission to do something, or that which has been approved.
ex: We will begin as soon as the boss says it's a go.
"Well, Tom, is it a go? You can trust me, for you'll have the thousand in your pocket before you start.[…]"

senses.d: An act; the working or operation.
The fashion or mode.
ex: quite the go
We are blowing each other out of the market with cheapness; but it is all the go, so we must not be behind the age.

senses.d: Noisy merriment.
ex: a high go

senses.d: Working correctly and ready to commence operation; approved and able to be put into action.
ex: John Glenn reports all systems are go.
"Life support system is go," said the earphone.

senses.d: A strategic board game, originally from China and today also popular in Japan and Korea, in which two players (black and white) attempt to control the largest area of the board with their counters.
